title: Darwin doesn't pick the best companies: why growth at all costs fails and values can drive growth
summary: "Survival of the fittest" means most prolific, not best. When growth rate is the only measure of fitness, profitability and betterment of humanity go unsolved. Cohen argues founders should let their values drive growth, citing Buffer, TOMS and USAA as examples.

principles.text: Growth is the right goal in winner-take-all markets, but growth at all costs is the problem.
principles.quote: There's nothing inherently wrong with obsessing over growth. In winner-take-all markets, growth is objectively the correct goal.

principles.text: If growth rate is your only fitness metric, other metrics like profitability stay unsolved.
principles.quote: When "growth rate" becomes the only important metric for company "fitness," other metrics are left unsolved.

principles.text: Winning the growth race is not a business model; many winners never convert from virus to business.
principles.quote: Many companies who won the growth battle never figure out how to convert themselves from a virus to a business.

principles.text: Don't trade growth off against values; use your values to drive growth.
principles.quote: The real question is not how to retard growth in submission to other values, but rather how to use our insistence values to drive growth.

principles.text: Transparency and positivity attract talent even at lower pay and with an undifferentiated product (Buffer).
principles.quote: talent nevertheless beats their door down to work there even in cases where they know ahead of time they'll take a pay-cut

principles.text: A mission people want to retell is a viral story that can beat a superior product (TOMS).
principles.quote: TOMS shoes is a massive success, not because of a superior product, but because of a viral story that people want to support and retell, exactly because its mission is so commendable and pure.
